intro: Knowing exactly when your dog needs each vaccine—and which ones—is the cornerstone of preventive pet health. Maternal antibodies block vaccines if given too early; missing boosters leaves gaps in immunity. This calculator applies the WSAVA (World Small Animal Veterinary Association) core vaccine framework: the **quintuple shot** (distemper, parvovirus, adenovirus-2, parainfluenza, leptospirosis) plus mandatory **rabies vaccination**. explanation:
## How the Vaccination Schedule Is Calculated

The calculator converts your dog's age to **weeks** (1 month = 4.345 weeks; 1 year = 52.14 weeks) and places it in one of four immunological windows:

| Age (weeks) | Stage | Main action |
|---|---|---|
| < 6 | Too young | Wait — maternal antibodies still active |
| 6–8 | Puppy: 1st dose | 1st quintuple vaccine |
| 9–12 | Puppy: 2nd dose | 2nd quintuple vaccine |
| 13–16 | Puppy: 3rd dose | 3rd quintuple + 1st rabies dose |
| 17–51 | Puppy: wrap-up | Any missed dose if delayed; plan 1st annual booster |
| ≥ 52, unvaccinated | Adult, no history | 2-dose series 3–4 weeks apart, then annual |
| ≥ 52, vaccinated | Adult on boosters | Annual booster (quintuple + rabies) |

---

### Why puppies need several doses

Maternal antibodies — absorbed through colostrum in the first 12–24 hours of life — actively neutralize vaccines because they can't tell an attenuated live virus from a real one. The problem is that their half-life varies significantly between individuals: in some puppies they fade by 6 weeks, in others they persist until 14–16 weeks.

That's why the **WSAVA (World Small Animal Veterinary Association)** and **AAHA (American Animal Hospital Association)** protocols call for 3–4 doses spaced 3–4 weeks apart, rather than a single early dose. The logic is statistical: at least one of those doses must fall within the **window of susceptibility** — the period when maternal antibodies no longer block the vaccine but the puppy hasn't yet been exposed to the pathogen in its environment.

The standard quintuple vaccine covers **distemper, infectious canine hepatitis, parvovirus, parainfluenza and leptospirosis**. Parvovirus is especially relevant: it has high mortality in puppies (up to 91% untreated, per veterinary studies), survives in the environment for up to 1 year, and requires the final dose of the series to be given at **16 weeks or later** to ensure seroconversion.

---

### Rabies vaccine timing

The rabies vaccine is effective from **12 weeks of age** (84 days). Before that age, a puppy's immune system does not mount a sufficiently protective response. Rabies vaccination is legally mandatory for dogs and cats in most countries. In Argentina, for example, it is required by national law (Ley 22.953), and SENASA — the national animal-health agency — runs free annual campaigns, typically between August and October, through registered veterinary clinics and municipal posts. Keeping the vaccination record current is a requirement at many parks and boarding kennels and for interprovincial travel certificates.

---

### Adult dogs with unknown history

If you adopted a dog with no vaccination record, the standard recommendation is to **restart the series from scratch** rather than assume prior immunity. The catch-up protocol for adults is:

- **Quintuple:** 2 doses 3–4 weeks apart (parvovirus in particular requires this initial booster even in adults with no documented history).
- **Rabies:** 1 dose, which can be given together with the first or second quintuple dose.
- **Maintenance:** annual booster of both vaccines.

Some vets run an **antibody titer test** (serology) before restarting the series in adults, especially if there is a risk of reaction or the animal is older. It is a valid option but does not replace an in-person clinical assessment.

---

### What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- **Optional non-core vaccines:** Bordetella bronchiseptica (kennel cough), leishmaniasis, Lyme (Borrelia), canine coronavirus. Whether they are indicated depends on lifestyle, geographic area and exposure to other animals.
- **Internal and external deworming:** it complements the vaccination schedule but follows a different plan (every 21 days in puppies up to 3 months, then quarterly or as directed).
- **Microchip:** mandatory in many jurisdictions; ideally implanted at the same time as the first vaccination.
- **Adjustments for clinical condition:** immunosuppressed animals, those on corticosteroid treatment, or pregnant females need an individual veterinary assessment before vaccination.

---

### Common mistakes when following the schedule

**Vaccinating before 6 weeks** produces no useful immunity and can interfere with the developing immune system. **Spacing doses more than 6 weeks apart** in the puppy series lengthens the risk window with no added immunological benefit. **Believing a single dose gives full protection** is the most common mistake: until all 3 doses of the series are complete and 7–14 days have passed since the last one, the puppy has no reliable protection against parvovirus or distemper. During that period, it is best to avoid contact with dogs of unknown history and high-traffic public surfaces.

---

> **Important:** this calculator offers general guidance based on the standard WSAVA and AAHA protocols. It does not replace assessment by a licensed veterinarian, who will adjust the plan according to the animal's individual health status and the local epidemiological situation.

faq.q: At what age should a puppy get its first vaccine?
faq.a: The first core vaccine (quintuple: distemper, parvovirus, adenovirus-2, parainfluenza, leptospirosis) is given between **6 and 8 weeks**. Before 6 weeks, maternal antibodies transferred via colostrum interfere with the immune response and the vaccine will not work reliably.

faq.q: How many doses does a puppy need in the first year?
faq.a: The WSAVA protocol calls for **3 doses** of the core vaccine at roughly 6–8, 9–12, and 13–16 weeks, followed by a first annual booster at 12 months. High-risk breeds (Rottweiler, Doberman) may receive a 4th dose at 16–20 weeks on veterinary advice. The rabies shot is added at the 13-week visit or later.

faq.q: Why can't I just give one vaccine and be done?
faq.a: Maternal antibodies from the mother's milk block vaccines unpredictably. By spacing 3 doses across the 6–16 week window, at least one dose is virtually guaranteed to trigger active immunity after those antibodies have faded. A single shot might land while maternal antibodies are still blocking it, leaving the puppy unprotected against life-threatening diseases like parvovirus.

faq.q: When does a puppy get its rabies shot?
faq.a: Rabies vaccine is appropriate from **12 weeks** of age. It is typically given at the same visit as the 3rd core dose. Annual boosters are required by law in most countries. In Argentina, SENASA organizes free public rabies campaigns generally between August and October.

faq.q: My adult dog has never been vaccinated. What do I do?
faq.a: Restart the series as if it were a first-time vaccination: administer **two doses of the quintuple vaccine 3–4 weeks apart** (this gap is critical for parvovirus protection) plus a rabies shot. After that, follow the standard annual booster schedule. Do not skip the two-dose series just because the dog is adult — prior natural exposure does not guarantee adequate antibody levels.

faq.q: How often do adult dogs need boosters?
faq.a: After the puppy series, most veterinary associations (WSAVA, AAHA) recommend the core vaccines **annually** as a minimum. Some protocols allow every 3 years for certain components (e.g., CDV, CPV, CAV) in dogs confirmed seropositive, but this requires titer testing. Rabies is typically required annually by law regardless. Always check your local regulations.

The quintuple vaccine (also called DA2PPL or DHPPL depending on the manufacturer) protects against five diseases in one injection: **Canine Distemper (D)**, **Adenovirus-2/Hepatitis (A2)**, **Parvovirus (P)**, **Parainfluenza (P)**, and **Leptospirosis (L)**. It is considered a core vaccine by WSAVA, meaning all dogs should receive it regardless of lifestyle.

faq.q: Are there vaccines beyond the quintuple that my dog might need?
faq.a: Yes. Non-core (optional) vaccines are given based on lifestyle and geographic risk: **Bordetella** (kennel cough) for dogs that visit kennels, groomers, or dog parks; **Giardia** in areas with high prevalence; **Leishmaniasis** in endemic regions. Your veterinarian will assess exposure risk at each annual visit.

faq.q: Can I vaccinate my dog at home to save money?
faq.a: In some countries, certain vaccines are sold over the counter. However, **self-vaccination carries significant risks**: improper handling breaks the cold chain (vaccines must stay at 2–8 °C), the lot number won't be officially recorded in the health booklet, and any adverse reaction (anaphylaxis can occur within minutes) requires immediate veterinary intervention. Rabies vaccination by a licensed veterinarian is legally required in most jurisdictions.

faq.q: What happens if I miss a vaccine dose?
faq.a: For the puppy series, if you miss the 2nd or 3rd dose by a few weeks, you can still administer it — you do **not** need to restart from zero. For adults, if the annual booster is more than 3 months overdue, most vets recommend administering a single catch-up dose. If it has been more than 2–3 years, a 2-dose series may be advisable. Ask your vet for a titer test if you are unsure about your dog's immunity status.
